To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the effects of media frames depend on the type of frame (media or audience), the type of audience (expert or layperson), the type of issue (familiar or unfamiliar), the type of media content (news, editorial, entertainment), and the media context (competition, monopoly).

(a) the framing of a news story is the result of a complex process involving the interaction of the journalists' and the audience's frames; (b) the framing process can be divided into four steps: frame building, framing of the news story, audience's framing and feedback from audience to journalists; (c) the audience's framing of a story is the result, in part, of the framing of the news by the journalists;

(1) the effects of media frames are mediated by individual level processes of meaning construction and (2) the effects of these processes on political attitudes and behavior are mediated by the way the media frame political issues.
In summary, our research is concerned with
a process that starts at the level of journalists (frame building) and ends with the level of journalists again (feedback loop).
how media frames affect the audience.
the process of framing as a process that takes place at the intersection of journalists and their audiences.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the effects of framing are mediated by the audience.
media frames are a product of the interaction between journalists and the political system.
framing is a theory of media effect, which can be used to describe and explain media effects on audiences.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the framing approach has the potential to provide a useful tool for the systematic study of media effects, but that the current state of framing research is far from fulfilling this potential.
we have developed a model that is more complete, more comprehensive and that has more explanatory power.
the framing process is a dynamic and interactive process, in which journalists and audiences are engaged in a continuous process of framing.
The main takeaway from our work is that
framing is best understood as an iterative process that involves the interplay between journalists, media, audiences and political actors.
framing is not a single phenomenon, but a family of phenomena that can be usefully classified into four types.
the framing process is not a one-directional process, and that the effects of media frames are mediated by audience frames.
